title: Robust Pre-Training by Adversarial Contrastive Learning
abstract: Recent work has shown that, when integrated with adversarial training, selfsupervised pre-training can lead to state-of-the-art robustness

question.a: Despite the remarkable advancements in self-supervised pre-training combined with adversarial training, existing approaches often fail to achieve a balance between robustness and generalizability. Previous studies primarily focus on either achieving robustness or optimizing contrastive learning independently, leaving a crucial gap in their joint optimization. This paper seeks to address this limitation by exploring how to effectively integrate adversarial contrastive learning to enhance overall robustness during the pre-training phase, ensuring improved performance across diverse scenarios.
question.b: Current self-supervised learning (SSL) in medical image analysis is mostly confined to single modalities, limiting its universality across different modalities. Joint SSL, which combines all modality data, faces challenges like modal data collision and high costs for integrating new knowledge. MedCoSS proposes a sequential pre-training approach to mitigate these issues, enhancing the model's generalization and scalability across various medical modalities.
question.c: Adversarial learning has shown success in various domains but applying it to pre-training LLMs is impractical due to high data and computational costs. ICL is effective but sensitive to prompt changes. adv-ICL addresses these issues by optimizing prompts in an adversarial manner without updating model parameters, making it computationally efficient and effective in low-resource settings.
question.d: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, hindering their reliable deployment. Existing defenses often involve cumbersome training processes or domain-specific heuristics, lacking efficiency and adaptability. This research addresses the open challenge of reprogramming well-trained models for robustness without parameter modification, offering an efficient and innovative approach to adversarial defenses.

title: Object-Region Video Transformers
abstract: Figure 1. Our ORViT model incorporates object information into video transformer layers. The figure shows the standard (uniformly spaced) transformer patch-tokens in blue, and object-regions corresponding to detections in orange. In ORViT any temporal patch-token (e.g., the patch in black at time T ) attends to all patch tokens (blue) and region tokens (orange). This allows the new patch representation to be informed by the objects. Our method shows strong performance improvement on multiple video understanding tasks and datasets, demonstrating the value of a model that incorporates object representations into a transformer architecture.

question.a: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have shown success in computer vision but struggle with dense prediction tasks due to limited inner-patch information interaction and feature scale diversity. Existing solutions often require costly pre-training. ViT-CoMer addresses these limitations by integrating multi-scale convolutional features into ViTs, enabling better local information interaction and multi-scale feature representation without the need for additional pre-training.
question.b: Existing video transformers often overlook the integration of object-specific information, which can hinder their performance in video understanding tasks. Although temporal patch-token methods provide some contextual awareness, they lack a mechanism to directly attend to object regions. This paper addresses this shortcoming by introducing the Object-Region Video Transformer (ORViT), which enhances patch representations through object-region interactions, thus offering a more nuanced understanding of dynamic video content.
question.c: Current VideoLLMs face challenges in detailed understanding of long-term videos due to overlooking local information and temporal structure. LongVLM addresses these limitations by proposing a method that preserves local details and integrates global context, aiming to enhance fine-grained video comprehension and response generation.
question.d: Video transformers are slow to train due to the large number of input tokens, many of which are redundant. Existing methods to reduce input tokens either have significant overhead, require dataset-specific tuning, or decrease accuracy. RLT addresses these limitations by being content-aware, requiring no tuning for different datasets, and being fast with negligible overhead, aiming to significantly accelerate and further scale video understanding.

title: Self-Supervised Learning from Images with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture
abstract: This paper demonstrates an approach for learning highly semantic image representations without relying on hand-crafted data-augmentations. We introduce the Imagebased Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA), a non-generative approach for self-supervised learning from images. The idea behind I-JEPA is simple: from a single context block, predict the representations of various target blocks in the same image. A core design choice to guide I-JEPA towards producing semantic representations is the masking strategy; specifically, it is crucial to (a) sample target blocks with sufficiently large scale (semantic), and to (b) use a sufficiently informative (spatially distributed) context block. Empirically, when combined with Vision Transformers, we find I-JEPA to be highly scalable. For instance, we train a ViT-Huge/14 on ImageNet using 16 A100 GPUs in under 72 hours to achieve strong downstream performance across a wide range of tasks, from linear classification to object counting and depth prediction.

question.a: Recent advancements in self-supervised learning and the training of large-scale foundation models have led to deep neural networks with significant capabilities. However, understanding what these models have learned and how to repurpose them for downstream tasks remains challenging. The paper addresses the need for interpretable analysis of neural networks and the development of techniques for leveraging their learned representations for additional tasks, without the need for annotated data or hyperparameter search.
question.b: Self-supervised learning has significantly advanced image representation but often relies on extensive hand-crafted data augmentations, which can be limiting and labor-intensive. Consequently, there is a gap in methods that provide effective learning without such dependencies. This paper seeks to address this challenge by proposing the Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA). By implementing a new approach to identify semantic representations without pre-defined augmentations, this research aims to enhance scalability and flexibility in image understanding tasks.
question.c: Self-supervised learning (SSL) models like DINOv2 have shown effectiveness in image classification but struggle with comprehensive image understanding tasks due to defective patch tokens. These defects, characterized by high-norm tokens, offer minimal local information and are largely image-independent. Current solutions require re-training the network from scratch, which is resource-intensive. This paper aims to understand and mitigate these defects more efficiently.
question.d: Current research in video self-supervised learning primarily focuses on representation learning for downstream tasks after supervised fine-tuning. However, there's a gap in directly learning useful tasks under self-supervised settings, especially in identifying and localizing changes that are monotonically correlated with time. This research aims to fill this gap by proposing a model that can discover and localize such changes without the need for manual supervision or subsequent fine-tuning.

title: Why Do Better Loss Functions Lead to Less Transferable Features?
abstract: Previous work has proposed many new loss functions and regularizers that improve test accuracy on image classification tasks. However, it is not clear whether these loss functions learn better representations for downstream tasks. This paper studies how the choice of training objective affects the transferability of the hidden representations of convolutional neural networks trained on ImageNet. We show that many objectives lead to statistically significant improvements in ImageNet accuracy over vanilla softmax cross-entropy, but the resulting fixed feature extractors transfer substantially worse to downstream tasks, and the choice of loss has little effect when networks are fully fine-tuned on the new tasks. Using centered kernel alignment to measure similarity between hidden representations of networks, we find that differences among loss functions are apparent only in the last few layers of the network. We delve deeper into representations of the penultimate layer, finding that different objectives and hyperparameter combinations lead to dramatically different levels of class separation. Representations with higher class separation obtain higher accuracy on the original task, but their features are less useful for downstream tasks. Our results suggest there exists a trade-off between learning invariant features for the original task and features relevant for transfer tasks. question.a: The field has seen significant progress in learning feature representations for various tasks, but there's a lack of theoretical understanding regarding compatible representations. This research addresses the challenge of maintaining alignment between different models trained with varying data, initialization seeds, loss functions, or architectures, crucial for minimizing the need for reprocessing gallery images in retrieval/search systems. The paper aims to establish a solid theoretical foundation for compatible representation learning and demonstrate its practical benefits in model replacement scenarios.
question.b: Vision-language models like CLIP have shown promise in zero-shot image classification, but efficient transfer learning (ETL) methods often overlook the challenge of varying transfer difficulties across tasks. Prior methods fail to adapt optimally to both high and low-difficulty domains, leading to suboptimal performance. This paper addresses this gap by proposing an adaptive ensemble method that leverages visual prompts and text adapters tailored to the difficulty of the target domain.
question.c: Neural networks have achieved remarkable performance in various tasks, but their robustness is crucial for safety-critical applications. Existing robustness benchmarks like ImageNet-C, ImageNet-9, and Stylized-ImageNet are limited in diversity and synthetic quality. ImageNet-D addresses these limitations by leveraging diffusion models to generate more diversified and realistic images, providing a rigorous benchmark for evaluating model robustness.
question.d: Numerous advancements in loss functions and regularizers have aimed to enhance test accuracy for image classification tasks. However, a critical gap persists regarding their efficacy in fostering transferable features for downstream applications. This study tackles the unclear relationship between the chosen training objectives and the representational quality of neural networks, ultimately revealing the trade-off between achieving high performance on the original task and maintaining feature relevance for transferability. Addressing this issue is essential for optimizing neural network architectures in applications beyond classification.

title: Graph Normalizing Flows
abstract: We introduce graph normalizing flows: a new, reversible graph neural network model for prediction and generation. On supervised tasks, graph normalizing flows perform similarly to message passing neural networks, but at a significantly reduced memory footprint, allowing them to scale to larger graphs. In the unsupervised case, we combine graph normalizing flows with a novel graph auto-encoder to create a generative model of graph structures. Our model is permutation-invariant, generating entire graphs with a single feed-forward pass, and achieves competitive results with the state-of-the art auto-regressive models, while being better suited to parallel computing architectures.

question.a: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a powerful tool for machine learning on graph-structured data. However, the question of size transferability—whether a GNN generalizes to larger graphs than those in the training set—has gained attention. Existing works on transferability have been almost exclusively limited to Message Passing GNNs (MPNNs), which are constrained by the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) graph isomorphism test. This paper addresses the limitations of MPNNs by extending generalization analyses to more powerful architectures like IGNs, which are at least as powerful as the k-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (k-WL) test.
question.b: Recent advancements in graph neural networks have mainly focused on message passing mechanisms, which can become memory-intensive. This limitation hampers their scalability to larger graphs, particularly in applications requiring high efficiency. This paper thus addresses the dual challenge of developing a reversible architecture that significantly reduces memory usage while maintaining competitive predictive performance and enhancing generative capabilities. By proposing graph normalizing flows, we aim to bridge this gap and facilitate more efficient processing of complex graph structures.
question.c: Convolutional GNNs have shown promise in various applications but suffer from limitations like limited expressiveness, over-smoothing, and over-squashing. These issues hinder their ability to model complex graph structures effectively. The paper aims to overcome these challenges by proposing a non-convolutional approach that leverages random walks and RNNs, offering a more expressive, robust, and efficient alternative to traditional GNNs.
question.d: Message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) have been successful in graph learning due to their respect for graph isomorphism invariance. However, MPNNs face limitations such as over-smoothing, over-squashing, and under-reaching of features. RWNNs offer an alternative approach but lack a principled understanding regarding their invariance, expressive power, and how they handle over-smoothing and over-squashing. This paper aims to address these gaps by providing a formal analysis of RWNNs, establishing their probabilistic invariance, and demonstrating their utility in graph learning tasks.

title: HierVL: Learning Hierarchical Video-Language Embeddings
abstract: Video-language embeddings are a promising avenue for injecting semantics into visual representations, but existing methods capture only short-term associations between seconds-long video clips and their accompanying text. We propose HierVL, a novel hierarchical video-language embedding that simultaneously accounts for both long-term and short-term associations. As training data, we take videos accompanied by timestamped text descriptions of human actions, together with a high-level text summary of the activity throughout the long video (as are available in Ego4D). We introduce a hierarchical contrastive training objective that encourages text-visual alignment at both the clip level and video level. While the clip-level constraints use the step-by-step descriptions to capture what is happening in that instant, the video-level constraints use the summary text to capture why it is happening, i.e., the broader context for the activity and the intent of the actor. Our hierarchical scheme yields a clip representation that outperforms its single-level counterpart as well as a long-term video representation that achieves SotA results on tasks requiring long-term video modeling. HierVL successfully transfers to multiple challenging downstream tasks (in EPIC-KITCHENS-100, Charades-Ego, HowTo100M) in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings.

question.a: Existing video-language embedding methods primarily focus on short-term associations between video clips and corresponding text, overlooking the critical long-term contextual relationships that influence understanding. This limitation hinders the effective modeling of dynamic human actions and intents within videos. By acknowledging the duality of short- and long-term associations, this paper proposes HierVL, addressing a pronounced gap in methods for hierarchical video-language modeling to enhance representation accuracy and improve performance on various downstream tasks.
question.b: Current VideoLLMs face challenges in detailed understanding of long-term videos due to overlooking local information and temporal structure. LongVLM addresses these limitations by proposing a method that preserves local details and integrates global context, aiming to enhance fine-grained video comprehension and response generation.
question.c: In-context learning is a significant capability of large language models (LLMs) that allows rapid adaptation to new tasks with minimal examples. However, current VLMs lack efficient in-context learning over video data, a crucial capability for tasks like recognizing novel or rare actions in videos. Existing video-based VLMs often fail to effectively reason over multiple frames or demonstrate in-context learning. This work addresses this gap by adapting distributional properties from text-based in-context learning to the video domain, aiming to enhance VLMs' ability to generalize to unseen video tasks.
question.d: Current Large Video-Language Models (LVidLMs) struggle with fine-grained spatial-temporal modeling, limiting their ability to understand or locate objects in detail within videos. The paper addresses this by proposing a trajectory-based alignment approach, aiming to improve video comprehension and performance on video-related multi-modal tasks.

title: Generalised Lipschitz Regularisation Equals Distributional Robustness
abstract: The problem of adversarial examples has highlighted the need for a theory of regularisation that is general enough to apply to exotic function classes, such as universal approximators. In response, we give a very general equality result regarding the relationship between distributional robustness and regularisation, as defined with a transportation cost uncertainty set. The theory allows us to (tightly) certify the robustness properties of a Lipschitz-regularised model with very mild assumptions. As a theoretical application we show a new result explicating the connection between adversarial learning and distributional robustness. We then give new results for how to achieve Lipschitz regularisation of kernel classifiers, which are demonstrated experimentally.

question.a: Adversarial robustness is a desirable property for neural networks, ensuring consistent predictions under small, often imperceptible, input perturbations. However, achieving this robustness typically requires specialized training schemes and access to large amounts of training data, which is often not feasible for off-the-shelf models. This paper addresses the challenge of robustifying these models without access to their training data, proposing a novel approach that utilizes text-to-image diffusion models for denoising and adaptation.
question.b: The emergence of adversarial examples underscores the necessity for comprehensive theories of regularization applicable to diverse function classes, particularly universal approximators. Notably, existing frameworks often lack the generality needed to assist in guaranteeing robustness across different models. This research addresses the critical gap by establishing a foundational equality between distributional robustness and regularization, thereby facilitating tight certification of Lipschitz-regularized models and enhancing our understanding of their robustness in complex scenarios.
question.c: Deep learning models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, despite their high accuracy. Randomized Smoothing (RS) offers a way to certify robustness but is inflexible and either degrades accuracy or only certifies against small attacks. ARS aims to improve robustness by providing test-time adaptivity while preserving rigorous bounds, addressing the limitations of existing adaptive defenses which are often heuristic and lack formal guarantees.
question.d: Adversarial Training (AT) has been used to improve the robustness of NLP models against adversarial attacks. However, the paper identifies a critical limitation: extreme miscalibration of models can mask gradients, leading to an illusion of robustness (IOR). This paper demonstrates that such robustness gains are superficial and proposes methods to mitigate this issue, emphasizing the importance of test-time temperature calibration in robustness evaluations.

title: Binge Watching: Scaling Affordance Learning from Sitcoms
abstract: In recent years, there has been a renewed interest in jointly modeling perception and action. At the core of this investigation is the idea of modeling affordances 1 . However, when it comes to predicting affordances, even the state of the art approaches still do not use any ConvNets. Why is that? Unlike semantic or 3D tasks, there still does not exist any large-scale dataset for affordances. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of creating one of the biggest dataset for learning affordances. We use seven sitcoms to extract a diverse set of scenes and how actors interact with different objects in the scenes. Our dataset consists of more than 10K scenes and 28K ways humans can interact with these 10K images. We also propose a two-step approach to predict affordances in a new scene. In the first step, given a location in the scene we classify which of the 30 pose classes is the likely affordance pose. In other words, it represents what actions can the object be used for.

question.a: Current VAD models, largely based on object detection pipelines, prioritize actor regions but often overlook essential contextual information necessary for accurate action classification. This paper addresses the challenge of improving classification in VAD, which is more complex than object classification due to the need for identifying fine-grained details in appearance and motion. The proposed model aims to reduce bias towards actor regions and encourage attention to context relevant to each action class, thereby advancing the field by improving classification accuracy and interpretability.
question.b: In-context learning is a significant capability of large language models (LLMs) that allows rapid adaptation to new tasks with minimal examples. However, current VLMs lack efficient in-context learning over video data, a crucial capability for tasks like recognizing novel or rare actions in videos. Existing video-based VLMs often fail to effectively reason over multiple frames or demonstrate in-context learning. This work addresses this gap by adapting distributional properties from text-based in-context learning to the video domain, aiming to enhance VLMs' ability to generalize to unseen video tasks.
question.c: Current video recognition models often learn scene-biased action representations due to spurious correlations between actions and scenes in training data, leading to poor performance on videos with unseen action-scene combinations. While scene-debiased models improve action recognition, they overlook valuable scene information. DEVIAS aims to overcome these limitations by learning disentangled representations of both action and scene, enabling robust performance across diverse scenarios and providing flexibility for downstream tasks.
question.d: Current efforts to model affordances have largely overlooked the need for comprehensive datasets that enable the effective training of convolutional networks. Despite notable advancements in perception and action modeling, the absence of a large-scale dataset specifically for affordance prediction remains a significant limitation. This paper seeks to bridge this gap by developing a dataset sourced from sitcoms, ensuring diverse interactions between actors and objects, thus facilitating the advancement of computational understanding of affordances in visual scenes.

title: Inverse Dynamics Pretraining Learns Good Representations for Multitask Imitation
abstract: In recent years, domains such as natural language processing and image recognition have popularized the paradigm of using large datasets to pretrain representations that can be effectively transferred to downstream tasks. In this work we evaluate how such a paradigm should be done in imitation learning, where both pretraining and finetuning data are trajectories collected by experts interacting with an unknown environment. Namely, we consider a setting where the pretraining corpus consists of multitask demonstrations and the task for each demonstration is set by an unobserved latent context variable. The goal is to use the pretraining corpus to learn a low dimensional representation of the high dimensional (e.g., visual) observation space which can be transferred to a novel context for finetuning on a limited dataset of demonstrations. Among a variety of possible pretraining objectives, we argue that inverse dynamics modeling -i.e., predicting an action given the observations appearing before and after it in the demonstration -is well-suited to this setting. We provide empirical evidence of this claim through evaluations on a variety of simulated visuomotor manipulation problems. While previous work has attempted various theoretical explanations regarding the benefit of inverse dynamics modeling, we find that these arguments are insufficient to explain the empirical advantages often observed in our settings, and so we derive a novel analysis using a simple but general environment model.

question.a: Current visual imitation learning methods struggle with generalization to unseen environments, often failing under minor perturbations like changes in lighting or object texture. This limitation stems from the high-dimensional and redundant nature of visual observation spaces. Stem-OB addresses these challenges by leveraging the semantic understanding capabilities of pretrained large image diffusion models to enhance the robustness and generalizability of VIL algorithms.
question.b: Recent work has shown in-context learning's compositional generalization capacity in large language models, but achieving this in LVLMs is challenging due to the asymmetry between visual and linguistic modalities, leading to redundant information in the visual modality. This redundancy affects demonstration selection and contextual information, hindering effective in-context learning. This paper aims to propose a method to achieve in-context compositional generalization in LVLMs by considering both content and structure of demonstrations.
question.c: Current Imitation Learning methods require extensive demonstrations and training for each new task, limiting their efficiency and scalability. The emergence of In-Context Learning in language and vision offers a promising direction for robotics, but lacks the large datasets available in those fields. Instant Policy addresses these challenges by introducing a graph-based representation and utilizing procedurally generated pseudo-demonstrations for training, aiming to enable rapid learning of new tasks with minimal demonstrations.
question.d: The field of imitation learning has yet to fully embrace pretraining paradigms effective in other areas such as natural language processing and image recognition. Notably, approaches that directly leverage multitask experience with unobserved latent contexts remain underexplored. This paper aims to resolve this gap by rigorously analyzing the appropriateness of inverse dynamics modeling for enhancing representation learning, thereby facilitating the transfer of learned policies across diverse tasks when finetuning on limited demonstration data.

title: Label Hallucination for Few-Shot Classification
abstract: Few-shot classification requires adapting knowledge learned from a large annotated base dataset to recognize novel unseen classes, each represented by few labeled examples. In such a scenario, pretraining a network with high capacity on the large dataset and then finetuning it on the few examples causes severe overfitting. At the same time, training a simple linear classifier on top of "frozen" features learned from the large labeled dataset fails to adapt the model to the properties of the novel classes, effectively inducing underfitting. In this paper we propose an alternative approach to both of these two popular strategies. First, our method pseudo-labels the entire large dataset using the linear classifier trained on the novel classes. This effectively "hallucinates" the novel classes in the large dataset, despite the novel categories not being present in the base database (novel and base classes are disjoint). Then, it finetunes the entire model with a distillation loss on the pseudo-labeled base examples, in addition to the standard cross-entropy loss on the novel dataset. This step effectively trains the network to recognize contextual and appearance cues that are useful for the novel-category recognition but using the entire large-scale base dataset and thus overcoming the inherent data-scarcity problem of few-shot learning. Despite the simplicity of the approach, we show that that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art on four wellestablished few-shot classification benchmarks.

question.a: Few-shot classification faces critical challenges in effectively utilizing large labeled datasets due to overfitting during fine-tuning and underfitting when using frozen features. Existing strategies inadequately address these issues, resulting in limited adaptability to novel classes. This paper seeks to bridge these gaps by proposing a novel method that combines pseudo-labeling with a distillation loss, thus leveraging the strengths of both approaches to mitigate data-scarcity and enhance recognition performance on unseen classes.
question.b: Current vision-language models like CLIP require domain-specific prompts for optimal performance in zero-shot classification tasks. These prompts are typically manually tuned, which is time-consuming and often suboptimal. The paper addresses this by proposing an unsupervised method to learn these prompts automatically, without the need for labeled data, thus advancing the field by making zero-shot classification more efficient and effective.
question.c: Current 3D few-shot segmentation methods require pre-training on 'seen' classes, which introduces time overhead and a domain gap on 'unseen' classes. This paper addresses these issues by proposing a training-free non-parametric network and a lightweight parametric variant that significantly reduces training time and mitigates domain gap issues.
question.d: Vision-language models like CLIP have shown remarkable potential in zero-shot and few-shot classification tasks. However, existing methods predominantly operate in an inductive setting, treating each query sample independently. This paper addresses the overlooked transductive setting, where joint predictions for a batch of query samples can leverage shared information, potentially improving accuracy. The research aims to fill the gap by developing a methodology tailored for CLIP that can significantly enhance performance in both zero-shot and few-shot scenarios.

title: MixUp Training Leads to Reduced Overfitting and Improved Calibration for the Transformer Architecture
abstract: MixUp is a computer vision data augmentation technique that uses convex interpolations of input data and their labels to enhance model generalization during training. However, the application of MixUp to the natural language understanding (NLU) domain has been limited, due to the difficulty of interpolating text directly in the input space. In this study, we propose MixUp methods at the Input, Manifold, and sentence embedding levels for the transformer architecture, and apply them to finetune the BERT model for a diverse set of NLU tasks. We find that MixUp can improve model performance, as well as reduce test loss and model calibration error by up to 50%.

question.a: The field of machine learning is shifting towards foundation models that can handle multiple tasks with minimal task-specific adaptations, inspired by the success of large language models (LLMs). However, vision tasks typically require specific modules, complicating the development of a general vision model. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a model that uses a simple multi-layer transformer architecture for various vision tasks, aiming to narrow the architectural gap between vision and language models.
question.b: Current approaches for dynamic representation learning in NLP often rely on pre-trained, temporally-agnostic models or recurrent methods, which suffer from overfitting and inefficiency. This paper introduces TempoFormer, a task-agnostic transformer-based model that addresses these limitations by jointly modeling intra- and inter-context dynamics with a novel temporal variation of positional embeddings.
question.c: Despite the demonstrated efficacy of MixUp in computer vision, its adoption within the natural language understanding domain remains limited due to challenges in direct text interpolation. Existing methods overlook the potential of applying MixUp at varied representation levels, such as input and sentence embeddings. Therefore, this paper seeks to bridge this gap by exploring MixUp strategies tailored for the transformer architecture, ultimately aiming to enhance model generalization and calibration in NLU tasks.
question.d: Transformers have revolutionized natural language processing, but their complex operations remain poorly understood. This study focuses on the inherent linearity of intermediate embedding transformations in transformer decoders, a largely unexplored aspect. The research aims to uncover new opportunities for model optimization, efficiency, and performance improvements by addressing this gap.

title: Guiding image captioning models toward more specific captions
abstract: Image captioning is conventionally formulated as the task of generating captions for images that match the distribution of reference image-caption pairs. However, reference captions in standard captioning datasets are short and may not uniquely identify the images they describe. These problems are further exacerbated when models are trained directly on image-alt text pairs collected from the internet. In this work, we show that it is possible to generate more specific captions with minimal changes to the training process. We implement classifier-free guidance

question.a: Retrieval-augmented image captioning models have shown success in generating captions by leveraging retrieved related captions, reducing model parameters and enabling better domain transfer. However, these models can be misled by irrelevant or incorrect information in the retrieved captions, leading to inaccurate generation. The robustness of such models, especially when multiple retrieved results are used, remains under-explored. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing the robustness of the SMALLCAP model and proposing methods to improve its resilience to noisy retrieved content.
question.b: Recent advancements in image captioning have explored text-only training methods to eliminate the need for paired image-text data, which is costly to obtain. However, existing methods often overlook the modality gap between text and image data, leading to performance degradation during inference. Additionally, reliance on external models for extra cues, such as object detectors or generated images, increases computational costs. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing cost-effective methods to acquire diverse information without additional models, aiming to improve zero-shot captioning performance significantly.
question.c: Image captioning often relies on reference captions that lack specificity and may inadequately represent the images. Consequently, models trained on generic datasets may struggle to produce uniquely identifying captions. The existing correlation between brevity in reference captions and decreased specificity highlights a significant gap. This paper addresses this issue by examining the potential for enhanced caption generation through minimal modifications to the training approach, which aims to fulfill the demand for more precise and informative captions.
question.d: Current automatic evaluation metrics for image captioning exhibit weak correlation with human judgments and struggle with handling hallucinations and generalizing across diverse images and texts. Recent data-driven metrics, while improved, still fall short due to their reliance on embeddings from unrelated tasks and limited settings. This research addresses these limitations by proposing a metric that integrates similarity-based and learning-based approaches, leveraging large-scale human feedback for training.

title: Few-Shot Class Incremental Learning with Attention-Aware Self-Adaptive Prompt
abstract: Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL) models aim to incrementally learn new classes with scarce samples while preserving knowledge of old ones. Existing FSCIL methods usually fine-tune the entire backbone, leading to overfitting and hindering the potential to learn new classes. On the other hand, recent prompt-based CIL approaches alleviate forgetting by training prompts with sufficient data in each task. In this work, we propose a novel framework named Attention-aware Self-adaptive Prompt (ASP). ASP encourages task-invariant prompts to capture shared knowledge by reducing specific information from the attention aspect. Additionally, self-adaptive task-specific prompts in ASP provide specific information and transfer knowledge from old classes to new classes with an Information Bottleneck learning objective. In summary, ASP prevents overfitting on base task and does not require enormous data in few-shot incremental tasks. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets validate that ASP consistently outperforms state-ofthe-art FSCIL and prompt-based CIL methods in terms of both learning new classes and mitigating forgetting.
