question.a: Current novel view synthesis methods rely heavily on 3D inductive biases, such as predefined 3D representations and rendering equations, which limit their flexibility and generalization to diverse scenarios. Recent advancements have reduced architecture-level biases but still depend on representation-level biases. LVSM aims to push the boundaries by adopting a fully data-driven approach, eliminating the need for predefined 3D structures and rendering equations, thus improving generalization and synthesis quality.
question.b: Fractal generative models have revealed potential in complex structure synthesis, yet existing frameworks are constrained by limited scalability and inefficient resource utilization. Despite their theoretical advantages, practical implementations often fall short in addressing parameter optimization for fractal representation. This paper seeks to bridge this significant gap by introducing innovative strategies to enhance the scalability of fractal models, enabling improved performance in generating intricate structures while efficiently leveraging computational resources.
question.c: Generative models in computer-aided drug design often produce molecules that are synthetically inaccessible. Current approaches either use synthetic complexity scores or perform synthesis planning post-generation, which are either oversimplified or computationally intensive. SynFlowNet addresses these limitations by incorporating forward synthesis constraints directly into the generative process, ensuring the generated molecules are synthesizable and diverse.
question.d: The field of generative modeling has seen significant advancements with models like VAEs, GANs, denoising diffusion models, and flow matching. However, these models are limited by their iterative step-wise nature and specific modalities. Generator Matching addresses these limitations by providing a unified framework that works across different data types and allows for the combination of models, expanding the design space to new Markov processes and enabling rigorous multimodal model construction.

title: Detect to Track and Track to Detect
abstract: Recent approaches for high accuracy detection and tracking of object categories in video consist of complex multistage solutions that become more cumbersome each year. In this paper we propose a ConvNet architecture that jointly performs detection and tracking, solving the task in a simple and effective way. Our contributions are threefold: (i) we set up a ConvNet architecture for simultaneous detection and tracking, using a multi-task objective for frame-based object detection and across-frame track regression; (ii) we introduce correlation features that represent object co-occurrences across time to aid the ConvNet during tracking; and (iii) we link the frame level detections based on our across-frame tracklets to produce high accuracy detections at the video level. Our ConvNet architecture for spatiotemporal object detection is evaluated on the large-scale ImageNet VID dataset where it achieves state-of-the-art results. Our approach provides better single model performance than the winning method of the last ImageNet challenge while being conceptually much simpler. Finally, we show that by increasing the temporal stride we can dramatically increase the tracker speed. Our code and models are available at

question.a: Current visual object tracking models are often designed for specific tasks, leading to limitations in handling diverse tracking scenarios and modalities. The paper addresses these limitations by proposing a general framework that leverages large-scale pretraining and parameter-efficient finetuning to unify various tracking tasks, aiming to improve performance and adaptability across different tracking benchmarks.
question.b: Current transformer-based lightweight object trackers often rely on pre-existing object detection architectures without optimizing for the unique demands of object tracking, leading to a trade-off between speed and accuracy. The paper addresses this gap by proposing a new method that significantly improves both tracking speed and accuracy, aiming to bridge the efficiency gap between fast and high-performance trackers.
question.c: Current video point tracking models face challenges with excessive computational demands due to brute-force correspondence matching across frames, leading to down-sampling of frame resolutions and loss of detailed visual features. This results in sub-optimal tracking accuracy, especially for intricate object parts. TrackIME addresses these limitations by focusing on important regions of frames without down-sampling, leveraging instance motion estimation and a unified framework for joint point tracking and segmentation to improve robustness to occlusions and enhance tracking performance.
question.d: Current object detection and tracking methods in video analysis increasingly rely on complex multistage solutions, resulting in cumbersome architectures that may hinder performance. Existing frameworks lack the efficiency necessary for real-time applications and often separate detection from tracking tasks. Hence, this research addresses the need for a straightforward yet effective architecture that integrates detection and tracking, aiming to simplify the process while maintaining, or even enhancing, accuracy and computational efficiency in spatiotemporal object identification.

title: FIT: Far-reaching Interleaved Transformers
abstract: We present FIT: a transformer-based architecture with efficient self-attention and adaptive computation. Unlike original transformers, which operate on a single sequence of data tokens, we divide the data tokens into groups, with each group being a shorter sequence of tokens. We employ two types of transformer layers: local layers operate on data tokens within each group, while global layers operate on a smaller set of introduced latent tokens. These layers, comprising the same set of self-attention and feed-forward layers as standard transformers, are interleaved, and cross-attention is used to facilitate information exchange between data and latent tokens within the same group. The attention complexity is O(n 2 ) locally within each group of size n, but can reach O(L 4 3 ) globally for sequence length of L. The efficiency can be further enhanced by relying more on global layers that perform adaptive computation using a smaller set of latent tokens. FIT is a versatile architecture and can function as an encoder, diffusion decoder, or autoregressive decoder. We provide initial evidence demonstrating its effectiveness in high-resolution image understanding and generation tasks. Notably, FIT exhibits potential in performing end-to-end training on gigabit-scale data, such as 6400×6400 images, or 160K tokens (after patch tokenization), within a memory capacity of 16GB, without requiring specific optimizations or model parallelism. 1

question.a: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have set new benchmarks in vision tasks but suffer from high computational complexity, especially with high-resolution images and long sequences. Recent NLP models with linear attention mechanisms offer efficiency and scalability, suggesting potential for similar advancements in vision tasks. This research addresses the need for a vision model that combines the strengths of ViTs with reduced computational demands, focusing on scalability, efficiency, and stability in training large models.
question.b: Transformers have revolutionized NLP and computer vision but suffer from high computational complexity, scaling quadratically with sequence length. This inefficiency is largely due to dense information flows between token representations, which introduce redundancy and unnecessary computations. SPARSEFLOW addresses this by optimizing sparse information flows, enabling significant speedup gains while maintaining accuracy, making it suitable for resource-constrained or real-time systems.
question.c: Transformer architectures have achieved state-of-the-art performance across various applications, but their attention operators suffer from quadratic computational complexity with respect to the number of tokens. This paper addresses the computational inefficiency by proposing a new attention operator derived from a variational form of the maximal coding rate reduction (MCR^2) objective, which does not require computing pairwise similarities between tokens.
question.d: Current transformer architectures primarily utilize fixed-length sequences, leading to inefficiencies in processing large datasets, particularly for high-resolution inputs. This design constrains adaptive computation methods, making it challenging to optimize performance while managing memory limitations. By introducing the FIT framework, which incorporates both local and global self-attention layers, this paper addresses the critical gap in achieving efficient data processing across variable token groupings, ultimately improving scalability for demanding tasks in image understanding and generation.

title: Big Bidirectional Insertion Representations for Documents
abstract: The Insertion Transformer is well suited for long form text generation due to its parallel generation capabilities, requiring O(log 2 n) generation steps to generate n tokens. However, modeling long sequences is difficult, as there is more ambiguity captured in the attention mechanism. This work proposes the Big Bidirectional Insertion Representations for Documents (Big BIRD), an insertionbased model for document-level translation tasks. We scale up the insertion-based models to long form documents. Our key contribution is introducing sentence alignment via sentence-positional embeddings between the source and target document. We show an improvement of +4.3 BLEU on the WMT'19 English→German document-level translation task compared with the Insertion Transformer baseline.

question.a: Current Transformer-based models struggle with long documents due to the quadratic scaling of attention mechanisms. Existing solutions like sparsifying attention, retrieval augmentation, or hierarchical processing have limitations. This research introduces NextLevelBERT, which processes text chunks at a higher semantic level, aiming to address these limitations by effectively modeling long-range dependencies without requiring token-level details.
question.b: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant capabilities in various NLP tasks, including translation, when fine-tuned. However, prior research lacks clarity on the exact amount of data needed for effective fine-tuning. This paper addresses whether minimal data, single translation direction, and noisy synthetic data can suffice for LLM fine-tuning in translation tasks. It aims to explore data efficiency, reduce resource-intensive practices, and uncover pitfalls in aligning LLMs for translation.
question.c: While LLMs have shown promise in various NLP tasks, their application in machine translation, particularly for open-source models, lags behind state-of-the-art NMT systems. The paper addresses this gap by leveraging the strengths of LLMs in contextual understanding and long-sequence processing. It aims to efficiently adapt LLMs for translation using parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques and to demonstrate their effectiveness in improving translation quality, especially in handling pronoun ambiguities and maintaining document coherence.
question.d: The challenge of accurately managing long-form document generation persists, largely due to the ambiguity captured in attention mechanisms of existing models. Despite the advances of the Insertion Transformer in parallel generation, limitations remain in effectively handling extensive sequences. This paper seeks to address this gap by scaling insertion-based models and introducing sentence-positional embeddings for enhanced alignment, thereby significantly improving performance on document-level translation tasks and contributing to the efficiency of translation systems.

title: nocaps: novel object captioning at scale Harsh Agrawal ˚1
abstract: Image captioning models have achieved impressive results on datasets containing limited visual concepts and large amounts of paired image-caption training data. However, if these models are to ever function in the wild, a much larger variety of visual concepts must be learned, ideally from less supervision. To encourage the development of image captioning models that can learn visual concepts from alternative data sources, such as object detection datasets, we present the first large-scale benchmark for this task. Dubbed 'nocaps', for novel object captioning at scale, our benchmark consists of 166,100 human-generated captions describing 15,100 images from the Open Images validation and test sets. The associated training data consists of COCO image-caption pairs, plus Open Images imagelevel labels and object bounding boxes. Since Open Images contains many more classes than COCO, nearly 400 object classes seen in test images have no or very few associated training captions (hence, nocaps). We extend existing novel object captioning models to establish strong baselines for this benchmark and provide analysis to guide future work.

question.a: Recent advancements in image captioning have explored text-only training methods to eliminate the need for paired image-text data, which is costly to obtain. However, existing methods often overlook the modality gap between text and image data, leading to performance degradation during inference. Additionally, reliance on external models for extra cues, such as object detectors or generated images, increases computational costs. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing cost-effective methods to acquire diverse information without additional models, aiming to improve zero-shot captioning performance significantly.
question.b: Current state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) rely on noisy web-scraped image-text datasets, resulting in incomplete and inconsistent descriptions. Existing dense human-written or model-generated caption datasets suffer from variations in human attention, bias, and hallucinations. This paper addresses these limitations by introducing a novel data-centric approach, ImageInWords, combining human annotators with machine-generated metadata to produce hyper-detailed, high-quality image descriptions.
question.c: Retrieval-augmented image captioning models have shown success in generating captions by leveraging retrieved related captions, reducing model parameters and enabling better domain transfer. However, these models can be misled by irrelevant or incorrect information in the retrieved captions, leading to inaccurate generation. The robustness of such models, especially when multiple retrieved results are used, remains under-explored. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing the robustness of the SMALLCAP model and proposing methods to improve its resilience to noisy retrieved content.
question.d: Image captioning models typically rely on limited visual concepts derived from substantial amounts of paired training data. As real-world applications demand broader understanding and reduced supervision, a critical gap emerges in the ability to learn new concepts from diverse data sources. Addressing this challenge, the nocaps benchmark fosters the exploration and enhancement of novel object captioning, facilitating improved model adaptability to previously unseen classes. This research paves the way for advancements in robust, scalable image captioning frameworks.

title: Multiview Pseudo-Labeling for Semi-supervised Learning from Video
abstract: We present a multiview pseudo-labeling approach to video learning, a novel framework that uses complementary views in the form of appearance and motion information for semi-supervised learning in video. The complementary views help obtain more reliable "pseudo-labels" on unlabeled video, to learn stronger video representations than from purely supervised data. Though our method capitalizes on multiple views, it nonetheless trains a model that is shared across appearance and motion input and thus, by design, incurs no additional computation overhead at inference time. On multiple video recognition datasets, our method substantially outperforms its supervised counterpart, and compares favorably to previous work on standard benchmarks in self-supervised video representation learning.

question.a: Current video object segmentation methods often rely on supervised learning with manual annotations or use optical flow for motion-based segmentation, which only captures instantaneous motion. This paper addresses the limitations of these approaches by leveraging long-term motion information from point trajectories, which can capture complex motion patterns over time, offering a more robust solution for unsupervised segmentation.
question.b: Multi-view multi-label learning is crucial for integrating diverse features and accurately capturing inter-label relationships. However, real-world data often suffer from incompleteness in views and labels, which most existing methods overlook. This paper addresses the double incompleteness challenge by proposing a method that not only generates missing views but also enhances the interaction between views and categories to improve classification performance.
question.c: Despite the advancements in semi-supervised learning for video, existing methods often underutilize complementary views, which hampers the extraction of robust features. Current frameworks typically overlook how joint training across different information types can lead to more reliable pseudo-labeling. This study addresses these limitations through a novel multiview pseudo-labeling approach, aiming to enhance the learning of video representations by effectively leveraging both appearance and motion data assemblages without incurring additional computational costs.
question.d: Current research in video self-supervised learning primarily focuses on representation learning for downstream tasks after supervised fine-tuning. However, there's a gap in directly learning useful tasks under self-supervised settings, especially in identifying and localizing changes that are monotonically correlated with time. This research aims to fill this gap by proposing a model that can discover and localize such changes without the need for manual supervision or subsequent fine-tuning.

title: Compositional Generalization via Neural-Symbolic Stack Machines
abstract: Despite achieving tremendous success, existing deep learning models have exposed limitations in compositional generalization, the capability to learn compositional rules and apply them to unseen cases in a systematic manner. To tackle this issue, we propose the Neural-Symbolic Stack Machine (NeSS). It contains a neural network to generate traces, which are then executed by a symbolic stack machine enhanced with sequence manipulation operations. NeSS combines the expressive power of neural sequence models with the recursion supported by the symbolic stack machine. Without training supervision on execution traces, NeSS achieves 100% generalization performance in four domains: the SCAN benchmark of language-driven navigation tasks, the task of few-shot learning of compositional instructions, the compositional machine translation benchmark, and context-free grammar parsing tasks.

question.a: Existing deep learning models have demonstrated significant success; however, they often fall short in compositional generalization, a vital skill for various applications. While some approaches attempt to address this, few effectively combine neural learning with systematic rule application. This paper focuses on this critical gap by introducing the Neural-Symbolic Stack Machine (NeSS), which leverages the strengths of both neural networks and symbolic systems to enhance compositional generalization without requiring execution trace supervision.
question.b: Compositionality is a fundamental property of natural language, enabling humans to process complex expressions based on understanding their parts. Despite significant progress in NLP, it remains unclear whether modern neural models exhibit human-like compositional behavior, especially during generalization. The paper addresses conflicting perspectives in the literature on how compositional behavior should be defined, evaluated, and achieved. It aims to provide a conceptual framework and survey researchers to identify consensus and open challenges in the field.
question.c: Current neural networks trained on form alone perform well on syntactic evaluations but struggle with hierarchical generalization, akin to human linguistic rules. The paper addresses whether adding semantic training signals can help these networks generalize hierarchically, similar to how children acquire language. This is important as it challenges the assumption that innate hierarchical biases are necessary for syntactic rule generalization.
question.d: Current deep learning models struggle with compositional generalization, especially when encountering new words, contexts, or syntactic structures not seen during training. Neurosymbolic methods aim to combine the strengths of neural and symbolic approaches but often suffer from scalability and flexibility issues. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a system where symbolic operations are performed in vector space, allowing for more efficient and flexible computations.

title: Universal halting times in optimization and machine learning
abstract: The authors present empirical distributions for the halting time (measured by the number of iterations to reach a given accuracy) of optimization algorithms applied to two random systems: spin glasses and deep learning. Given an algorithm, which we take to be both the optimization routine and the form of the random landscape, the fluctuations of the halting time follow a distribution that, after centering and scaling, remains unchanged even when the distribution on the landscape is changed. We observe two qualitative classes: A Gumbel-like distribution that appears in Google searches, human decision times, the QR eigenvalue algorithm and spin glasses, and a Gaussian-like distribution that appears in conjugate gradient method, deep network with MNIST input data and deep network with random input data. This empirical evidence suggests presence of a class of distributions for which the halting time is independent of the underlying distribution under some conditions.

question.a: Current optimization methods in machine learning often rely on learning rate schedules that require setting a stopping time T in advance, which is a limitation. The paper addresses this by proposing a method that does not need T, thus bridging the gap between theoretical optimality and practical performance.
question.b: Recent advancements in deep learning have shown that regularizing second-order information can improve model generalization. However, methods like weight noise and gradient penalties have shown inconsistent results. The paper addresses this inconsistency by highlighting the importance of the NME matrix, which has been largely overlooked in previous studies. The research aims to provide empirical and theoretical evidence that the NME is crucial for understanding the performance of gradient penalties and their sensitivity to activation functions, as well as the difference in regularization performance between gradient penalties and weight noise.
question.c: While empirical investigations into halting times in optimization have been conducted, a systematic understanding of the independence of halting time distributions from underlying landscape characteristics remains lacking. This study addresses this gap by revealing the properties of Gumbel-like and Gaussian-like distributions observed in distinct optimization contexts. By elucidating the conditions under which halting times consistently manifest these properties, the research contributes valuable insights to the theory of optimization and deep learning, which could enhance algorithmic design and analysis.
question.d: The manifold hypothesis is widely accepted in high-dimensional data analysis, with empirical evidence supporting its validity across various domains. However, there is a lack of formal results on how encoding geometric structure affects the learnability of neural networks. Previous research has established hardness results for learning neural networks under i.i.d. Gaussian or uniform Boolean data distributions. This paper addresses the gap by examining the learnability of neural networks under the manifold hypothesis, aiming to identify minimal assumptions on the curvature and regularity of the manifold that render the learning problem efficiently learnable.

title: Non-Autoregressive Machine Translation with Latent Alignments
abstract: This paper presents two strong methods, CTC and Imputer, for non-autoregressive machine translation that model latent alignments with dynamic programming. We revisit CTC for machine translation and demonstrate that a simple CTC model can achieve state-of-theart for single-step non-autoregressive machine translation, contrary to what prior work indicates. In addition, we adapt the Imputer model for non-autoregressive machine translation and demonstrate that Imputer with just 4 generation steps can match the performance of an autoregressive Transformer baseline. Our latent alignment models are simpler than many existing non-autoregressive translation baselines; for example, we do not require target length prediction or re-scoring with an autoregressive model. On the competitive WMT'14 En→De task, our CTC model achieves 25.7 BLEU with a single generation step, while Imputer achieves 27.5 BLEU with 2 generation steps, and 28.0 BLEU with 4 generation steps. This compares favourably to the autoregressive Transformer baseline at 27.8 BLEU. * Equal contribution. † Work done as part of the Google AI Residency.

question.a: Large language models (LLMs) have shown significant capabilities in various NLP tasks, including translation, when fine-tuned. However, prior research lacks clarity on the exact amount of data needed for effective fine-tuning. This paper addresses whether minimal data, single translation direction, and noisy synthetic data can suffice for LLM fine-tuning in translation tasks. It aims to explore data efficiency, reduce resource-intensive practices, and uncover pitfalls in aligning LLMs for translation.
question.b: While LLMs have shown promise in various NLP tasks, their application in machine translation, particularly for open-source models, lags behind state-of-the-art NMT systems. The paper addresses this gap by leveraging the strengths of LLMs in contextual understanding and long-sequence processing. It aims to efficiently adapt LLMs for translation using parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques and to demonstrate their effectiveness in improving translation quality, especially in handling pronoun ambiguities and maintaining document coherence.
question.c: Current LLM fine-tuning methods for simultaneous translation rely on prompting optimization, which suffers from computational inefficiency, increased prompt sizes, and fine-tuning-inference mismatches. These limitations hinder the practical deployment of LLMs for real-time translation tasks. SimulMask aims to provide a more efficient and flexible paradigm for fine-tuning LLMs, reducing computational costs while improving translation quality.
question.d: Non-autoregressive machine translation has advanced rapidly, yet multiple approaches still involve complex models requiring target length prediction and re-scoring. Despite existing progress, significant gaps remain in simplifying model architectures without sacrificing performance. This paper addresses these limitations by introducing the CTC and Imputer methods, which leverage latent alignments through dynamic programming. By focusing on streamlined processing, the proposed models aim to enhance translation efficiency while maintaining competitive results against autoregressive baselines.

title: 3D human pose estimation in video with temporal convolutions and semi-supervised training
abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that 3D poses in video can be effectively estimated with a fully convolutional model based on dilated temporal convolutions over 2D keypoints. We also introduce back-projection, a simple and effective semi-supervised training method that leverages unlabeled video data. We start with predicted 2D keypoints for unlabeled video, then estimate 3D poses and finally back-project to the input 2D keypoints. In the supervised setting, our fully-convolutional model outperforms the previous best result from the literature by 6 mm mean per-joint position error on Human3.6M, corresponding to an error reduction of 11%, and the model also shows significant improvements on HumanEva-I. Moreover, experiments with back-projection show that it comfortably outperforms previous state-of-the-art results in semisupervised settings where labeled data is scarce. Code and models are available at

question.a: Despite advancements in 3D human pose estimation, existing methods primarily rely on supervised training, which limits their applicability in scenarios with sparse labeled data. Additionally, traditional approaches often overlook the potential of semi-supervised techniques to leverage abundant unlabeled video data. This paper addresses these gaps by introducing a novel back-projection method that enhances the utility of unlabeled video information, thereby improving pose estimation accuracy in semi-supervised settings and broadening the practical applications of the technology.
question.b: Current 3D Human Pose Estimation (3D HPE) methods face challenges such as depth ambiguity, complex human body structures, and limited generalizability due to restricted action classes in datasets. FinePOSE addresses these issues by incorporating fine-grained part-aware prompts and diffusion models to improve denoising quality and estimation accuracy, aiming to advance the field by providing more precise and adaptable 3D pose predictions.
question.c: Current egocentric 3D human pose estimation methods face challenges with depth ambiguity and self-occlusion, especially in complex poses. Existing stereo methods do not fully utilize their settings and lack consideration of scene information, limiting their accuracy. This research aims to overcome these limitations by proposing a novel framework that enhances pose estimation accuracy through scene reconstruction and temporal feature integration.
question.d: Transformer-based architectures have achieved state-of-the-art performance in video-based 3D human pose estimation but suffer from high computational demands due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention with respect to the number of tokens (frames). This paper addresses the challenge of deploying these models on resource-constrained devices by proposing a method that prunes redundant pose tokens and recovers full-length tokens, aiming to maintain a large temporal receptive field for accurate estimation while improving efficiency.

title: Exploring Randomly Wired Neural Networks for Image Recognition
abstract: Neural networks for image recognition have evolved through extensive manual design from simple chain-like models to structures with multiple wiring paths. The success of ResNets [11]  and DenseNets

question.a: Neural pruning is a technique to compress and accelerate deep neural networks by identifying optimal subnetworks within a specified sparsity budget. Current methods face challenges in minimizing performance drop while achieving desired sparsity. The paper addresses these challenges by analyzing the evolution of optimal subnetworks' population under continuous sparsity increments from a thermodynamics perspective, aiming to provide a mathematically tractable approach for neural pruning.
question.b: Neural networks have achieved remarkable performance in various tasks, but their robustness is crucial for safety-critical applications. Existing robustness benchmarks like ImageNet-C, ImageNet-9, and Stylized-ImageNet are limited in diversity and synthetic quality. ImageNet-D addresses these limitations by leveraging diffusion models to generate more diversified and realistic images, providing a rigorous benchmark for evaluating model robustness.
question.c: The field of deep learning lacks a unified tool that connects architecture, data, and inductive biases in an interpretable way. Current approaches to architecture design are fragmented, relying on heuristic-based modifications, biology-inspired design, or efficiency and stability considerations. This paper addresses this gap by focusing on the geometry of neural networks in the input space, aiming to provide a model for the inductive biases of neural architectures.
question.d: Despite the advancements in neural network architectures for image recognition, the potential of randomly wired networks remains underexplored. Current methods rely heavily on deterministic wiring strategies, limiting innovation in design flexibility and efficiency. This research aims to bridge this gap by investigating the effectiveness of randomness in neural connections, thereby uncovering novel structural configurations that could enhance image recognition performance and broaden our understanding of neural architecture optimization.

title: Understanding and Improving Robustness of Vision Transformers through Patch-based Negative Augmentation
abstract: We investigate the robustness of vision transformers (ViTs) through the lens of their special patch-based architectural structure, i.e., they process an image as a sequence of image patches. We find that ViTs are surprisingly insensitive to patchbased transformations, even when the transformation largely destroys the original semantics and makes the image unrecognizable by humans. This indicates that ViTs heavily use features that survived such transformations but are generally not indicative of the semantic class to humans. Further investigations show that these features are useful but non-robust, as ViTs trained on them can achieve high in-distribution accuracy, but break down under distribution shifts. From this understanding, we ask: can training the model to rely less on these features improve ViT robustness and out-of-distribution performance? We use the images transformed with our patch-based operations as negatively augmented views and offer losses to regularize the training away from using non-robust features. This is a complementary view to existing research that mostly focuses on augmenting inputs with semantic-preserving transformations to enforce models' invariance. We show that patch-based negative augmentation consistently improves robustness of ViTs on ImageNet based robustness benchmarks across 20+ different experimental settings. Furthermore, we find our patch-based negative augmentation are complementary to traditional (positive) data augmentation techniques and batchbased negative examples in contrastive learning.

question.a: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have shown success in computer vision but struggle with dense prediction tasks due to limited inner-patch information interaction and feature scale diversity. Existing solutions often require costly pre-training. ViT-CoMer addresses these limitations by integrating multi-scale convolutional features into ViTs, enabling better local information interaction and multi-scale feature representation without the need for additional pre-training.
question.b: Patch-level data augmentation techniques like Cutout and CutMix have shown significant empirical success in improving generalization in vision tasks. However, there is a lack of comprehensive theoretical understanding of why and how these methods work. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing a theoretical analysis of these techniques, demonstrating their ability to learn features that vanilla training cannot, and establishing CutMix as the most effective method among the three for learning all features, including extremely rare ones.
question.c: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have set new benchmarks in vision tasks but suffer from high computational complexity, especially with high-resolution images and long sequences. Recent NLP models with linear attention mechanisms offer efficiency and scalability, suggesting potential for similar advancements in vision tasks. This research addresses the need for a vision model that combines the strengths of ViTs with reduced computational demands, focusing on scalability, efficiency, and stability in training large models.
question.d: Despite advances in training vision transformers (ViTs), their surprising insensitivity to significant semantic-disruptive patch transformations exposes a critical limitation in their robustness. This phenomenon raises concerns about their reliance on non-robust features, which can undermine performance under distribution shifts. By addressing the gap in training methodologies focused on non-robust features, this paper explores patch-based negative augmentation, a unique approach intended to enhance the resilience of ViTs, providing insights for more effective model training.

title: MoDE: CLIP Data Experts via Clustering
abstract: The success of contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) relies on the supervision from the pairing between images and captions, which tends to be noisy in webcrawled data. We present Mixture of Data Experts (MoDE) and learn a system of CLIP data experts via clustering. Each data expert is trained on one data cluster, being less sensitive to false negative noises in other clusters. At inference time, we ensemble their outputs by applying weights determined through the correlation between task metadata and cluster conditions. To estimate the correlation precisely, the samples in one cluster should be semantically similar, but the number of data experts should still be reasonable for training and inference. As such, we consider the ontology in human language and propose to use finegrained cluster centers to represent each data expert at a coarse-grained level. Experimental studies show that four CLIP data experts on ViT-B/16 outperform the ViT-L/14 by OpenAI CLIP and OpenCLIP on zero-shot image classification but with less (<35%) training cost. Meanwhile, MoDE can train all data expert asynchronously and can flexibly include new data experts. The code is available at

question.a: Contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) is hindered by the noisy supervision typical of webcrawled datasets, adversely affecting model performance. Current approaches do not efficiently mitigate this noise across diverse data clusters, resulting in suboptimal outcomes. This paper addresses the challenge of standardizing data influence within CLIP by introducing a method that employs clustering to dynamically generate data experts. This improvement allows for reduced sensitivity to false negations and enhances semantic correlation during training and inference.
question.b: Auto-regressive text-to-image generation methods, facilitated by image tokenizers, have not leveraged pre-trained language models, unlike diffusion-based models which benefit from them. This paper investigates this gap, addressing why pre-trained language models do not enhance auto-regressive text-to-image generation, highlighting the semantic differences between image and text tokens and the simplicity of text in image-text datasets.
question.c: Current Vision-Language (VL) models rely on large-scale pre-training on web-collected data, requiring high-capacity architectures and significant computational resources. Despite their success, these models are generalist, leading to inefficiencies when the target domain is known. This paper addresses the need for domain-specific pre-training, focusing on human activities, to improve efficiency and accuracy while preserving generalist capabilities.
question.d: Vision-language models like CLIP have shown strong zero-shot performance but are limited by their size and inefficient inference. Knowledge distillation offers a solution but typically requires original data, which is not always available due to copyright and privacy concerns. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a data-free knowledge distillation method that allows for customization based on arbitrary class texts or few example images, without the need for original data.

title: Transformers without Normalization
abstract: Normalization layers are ubiquitous in modern neural networks and have long been considered essential. This work demonstrates that Transformers without normalization can achieve the same or better performance using a remarkably simple technique. We introduce Dynamic Tanh (DyT), an element-wise operation DyT(x) = tanh(αx), as a drop-in replacement for normalization layers in Transformers. DyT is inspired by the observation that layer normalization in Transformers often produces tanh-like, S-shaped input-output mappings. By incorporating DyT, Transformers without normalization can match or exceed the performance of their normalized counterparts, mostly without hyperparameter tuning. We validate the effectiveness of Transformers with DyT across diverse settings, ranging from recognition to generation, supervised to self-supervised learning, and computer vision to language models. These findings challenge the conventional understanding that normalization layers are indispensable in modern neural networks, and offer new insights into their role in deep networks.

question.a: The field of deep learning lacks a unified tool that connects architecture, data, and inductive biases in an interpretable way. Current approaches to architecture design are fragmented, relying on heuristic-based modifications, biology-inspired design, or efficiency and stability considerations. This paper addresses this gap by focusing on the geometry of neural networks in the input space, aiming to provide a model for the inductive biases of neural architectures.
question.b: Normalization layers have long been deemed essential for the performance of neural networks, particularly in Transformers. However, the assumption that such layers are indispensable has not been adequately scrutinized. This paper addresses the gap by proposing Dynamic Tanh (DyT) as an alternative that can achieve comparable, if not superior, performance without normalization. By challenging established norms, this research opens new avenues for understanding the role and necessity of normalization in deep learning architectures.
question.c: Despite the transformative impact of transformers in AI, the theoretical understanding of these models, especially regarding the representations developed and the effect of hyperparameters, remains limited. This paper addresses the gap by studying the intermediate clustering phases before the system collapses to a single cluster, which is crucial for understanding the development of representations in deep models and their effectiveness.
question.d: Despite the advancements in convolutional networks (ConvNets) and Transformers, ConvNets retain robust performance and efficiency for various tasks. However, the slow speed and convergence issues of Deformable Convolution v3 (DCNv3) limit its application. DCNv4 aims to address these limitations by enhancing dynamic properties and optimizing memory access, thereby improving speed and performance.

title: Navigation World Models
abstract: Figure 1. We train a Navigation World Model (NWM) from video footage of robots and their associated navigation actions (a). After training, NWM can evaluate trajectories by synthesizing their videos and scoring the final frame's similarity with the goal (b). We use NWM to plan from scratch or rank experts navigation trajectories, improving downstream visual navigation performance. In unknown environments, NWM can simulate imagined trajectories from a single image (c). In all examples above, the input to the model is the first image and actions, then the model auto-regressively synthesizes future observations. Click on the image to view examples in a browser.

question.a: The development of autonomous vehicles (AVs) heavily relies on simulation for training and evaluation due to the risks of real-world testing. While visual aspects of simulators have advanced, generating realistic and controllable agent behavior remains challenging. Traditional methods often fail to generate unseen scenarios and lack the ability to incorporate specific conditions for targeted training. RealGen addresses these limitations by proposing a novel framework that enhances scenario generation with retrieval-augmented techniques, offering flexibility and controllability in generating traffic scenarios.
question.b: Robust navigation in unknown environments remains a significant challenge for robotic systems, primarily due to the inadequacy of existing models in planning and evaluating trajectories. Current approaches often struggle with incorporating real-time feedback from dynamic visual inputs, leading to suboptimal performance in complex navigation tasks. This paper addresses the limitations in assessing trajectory quality through similarity measures and introduces a Navigation World Model capable of simulating groups of imagined trajectories, enhancing evaluative accuracy and strategic planning for improved navigation efficacy.
question.c: Current image-goal navigation methods suffer from inefficient exploration due to the use of all historical observations without considering goal relevance. MemoNav addresses this by introducing a memory model that selectively retains informative scene features, enhancing navigation efficiency and performance.
question.d: Current VLN tasks face challenges in accurately representing future environments due to visual occlusions and the computational cost of generating high-resolution images. Existing methods suffer from image distortion and inefficiency. This research aims to overcome these limitations by predicting multi-level semantic features for future environments, enhancing the agent's ability to make informed navigation decisions.

title: Transformer visualization via dictionary learning: contextualized embedding as a linear superposition of transformer factors
abstract: Transformer networks have revolutionized NLP representation learning since they were introduced. Though a great effort has been made to explain the representation in transformers, it is widely recognized that our understanding is not sufficient. One important reason is that there lack enough visualization tools for detailed analysis. In this paper, we propose to use dictionary learning to open up these 'black boxes' as linear superpositions of transformer factors. Through visualization, we demonstrate the hierarchical semantic structures captured by the transformer factors, e.g., word-level polysemy disambiguation, sentence-level pattern formation, and long-range dependency. While some of these patterns confirm the conventional prior linguistic knowledge, the rest are relatively unexpected, which may provide new insights. We hope this visualization tool can bring further knowledge and a better understanding of how transformer networks work. The code is available at

question.a: Transformers have revolutionized natural language processing, but their complex operations remain poorly understood. This study focuses on the inherent linearity of intermediate embedding transformations in transformer decoders, a largely unexplored aspect. The research aims to uncover new opportunities for model optimization, efficiency, and performance improvements by addressing this gap.
question.b: Despite significant advancements in transformer networks for NLP representation learning, our understanding of their inner workings remains limited, primarily due to insufficient visualization tools. Existing approaches do not adequately reveal the complexities of learned representations, hindering meaningful analysis. This paper addresses this critical gap by employing dictionary learning to deconstruct transformer representations into linear superpositions, thereby facilitating a deeper exploration of the hierarchical semantic structures they embody.
question.c: The field of natural language processing has seen significant advancements with Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the computational complexity of Transformer architectures remains a bottleneck for processing long sequences. While alternatives like Linear Transformers and State Space Models (SSMs) offer improvements, they still lag behind in In-Context Learning capabilities. The Based model, a hybrid of Linear Transformer and convolutional networks, showed promise but had limitations with long contexts. This research aims to address these limitations by refining the kernel function and incorporating new architectural modifications to improve In-Context Learning and overall language modeling performance.
question.d: Transformers are state-of-the-art in NLP, but their inner workings remain opaque, especially in unsupervised tasks like information retrieval. While explainable AI has advanced, it has primarily focused on supervised models. This paper addresses the gap by leveraging second-order explanations to analyze feature interactions in Transformer-based similarity models, providing deeper insights into their predictions and uncovering patterns in semantic similarity tasks.

title: Long-Short Temporal Contrastive Learning of Video Transformers
abstract: Video transformers have recently emerged as a competitive alternative to 3D CNNs for video understanding. However, due to their large number of parameters and reduced inductive biases, these models require supervised pretraining on large-scale image datasets to achieve top performance. In this paper, we empirically demonstrate that selfsupervised pretraining of video transformers on video-only datasets can lead to action recognition results that are on par or better than those obtained with supervised pretraining on large-scale image datasets, even massive ones such as ImageNet-21K. Since transformer-based models are effective at capturing dependencies over extended temporal spans, we propose a simple learning procedure that forces the model to match a long-term view to a short-term view of the same video. Our approach, named Long-Short Temporal Contrastive Learning (LSTCL), enables video transformers to learn an effective clip-level representation by predicting temporal context captured from a longer temporal extent. To demonstrate the generality of our findings, we implement and validate our approach under three different self-supervised contrastive learning frameworks (MoCo v3, BYOL, SimSiam) using two distinct video-transformer architectures, including an improved variant of the Swin Transformer augmented with space-time attention. We conduct a thorough ablation study and show that LSTCL achieves competitive performance on multiple video benchmarks and represents a convincing alternative to supervised image-based pretraining.

question.a: In-context learning is a significant capability of large language models (LLMs) that allows rapid adaptation to new tasks with minimal examples. However, current VLMs lack efficient in-context learning over video data, a crucial capability for tasks like recognizing novel or rare actions in videos. Existing video-based VLMs often fail to effectively reason over multiple frames or demonstrate in-context learning. This work addresses this gap by adapting distributional properties from text-based in-context learning to the video domain, aiming to enhance VLMs' ability to generalize to unseen video tasks.
question.b: Current research in video self-supervised learning primarily focuses on representation learning for downstream tasks after supervised fine-tuning. However, there's a gap in directly learning useful tasks under self-supervised settings, especially in identifying and localizing changes that are monotonically correlated with time. This research aims to fill this gap by proposing a model that can discover and localize such changes without the need for manual supervision or subsequent fine-tuning.
question.c: Video transformers offer a novel method for video understanding but face significant challenges in requiring extensive supervised pretraining on large image datasets, which limits their accessibility and practicality. Existing approaches fall short in leveraging the full potential of video data for self-supervised training. This paper addresses this significant gap by introducing Long-Short Temporal Contrastive Learning, which enables effective learning of temporal contexts from video-only datasets, thus enhancing the performance of video transformers without dependency on conventional image pretraining.
question.d: Video transformers are slow to train due to the large number of input tokens, many of which are redundant. Existing methods to reduce input tokens either have significant overhead, require dataset-specific tuning, or decrease accuracy. RLT addresses these limitations by being content-aware, requiring no tuning for different datasets, and being fast with negligible overhead, aiming to significantly accelerate and further scale video understanding.

question.a: Current multimodal sentence embedding methods, while promising, suffer from noisy negative samples that can hinder performance. Additionally, the variation within negative pairs is often overlooked, limiting the discriminative power of the embeddings. This research addresses these issues by introducing a knowledge distillation approach and an adaptive angular margin contrastive learning objective, aiming to improve the accuracy and robustness of sentence embeddings in multimodal settings.
question.b: Contrastive learning has driven significant progress in STS tasks, with leading methods achieving an average Spearman's correlation score of around 86 on seven STS benchmarks. However, further improvements have stalled, with no method exceeding 86.5. The paper identifies that the core limitation is the binary classification nature of contrastive learning, which restricts the Spearman correlation upper bound to 87.5. Pcc-tuning aims to overcome this by utilizing fine-grained data and a more nuanced loss function, thereby advancing the field.
question.c: Current dense contrastive representation learning approaches often rely on a singular global representation of an image, which limits their ability to capture local features effectively. This paper aims to address the gap in utilizing dense negative pairs, which can enhance the learning process by incorporating finer detail and context within the representation. By refining how dense contrastive learning is applied, we aspire to improve representation accuracy and ultimately contribute to broader advancements in visual understanding.
question.d: Current generative models, particularly diffusion models, have shown powerful capabilities in generating vivid samples but have been less explored for discriminative tasks. Representation learning is crucial for these tasks, aiming to extract useful information for building classifiers or predictors. The paper addresses the gap by proposing a method that leverages the denoising process from generative tasks to improve feature discrimination in discriminative tasks, without additional computational costs.

title: EGO-TOPO: Environment Affordances from Egocentric Video
abstract: First-person video naturally brings the use of a physical environment to the forefront, since it shows the camera wearer interacting fluidly in a space based on his intentions. However, current methods largely separate the observed actions from the persistent space itself. We introduce a model for environment affordances that is learned directly from egocentric video. The main idea is to gain a human-centric model of a physical space (such as a kitchen) that captures (1) the primary spatial zones of interaction and (2) the likely activities they support. Our approach decomposes a space into a topological map derived from first-person activity, organizing an ego-video into a series of visits to the different zones. Further, we show how to link zones across multiple related environments (e.g., from videos of multiple kitchens) to obtain a consolidated representation of environment functionality. On EPIC-Kitchens and EGTEA+, we demonstrate our approach for learning scene affordances and anticipating future actions in long-form video. Project page: In Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2020.

question.a: Current RVOS tasks rely on static attributes like object names, which are insufficient in complex scenarios with similar redundant objects or changing object states. ActionVOS addresses these limitations by using human actions as prompts, which precisely describe human behavior and help identify objects involved in interactions and understand state changes. This research is important for advancing egocentric vision applications by improving the segmentation of active objects in videos.
question.b: First-person video captures interactions within environments, yet existing methods fail to integrate observed actions with the structural characteristics of those spaces. Notably, the dearth of human-centric models that accurately depict spatial zones and their associated activities represents a critical gap. This study aims to advance understanding by exploring a consolidated representation of environment functionality, thereby enabling improved learning of scene affordances and anticipatory action in egocentric contexts.
question.c: Current Large Language Models (LLMs) and Visual Large Language Models (VLLMs) have limitations in providing directly applicable instructions for human skill transfer and in generating images that align with the user's egocentric perspective. The paper addresses these limitations by proposing a method to enrich action descriptions and improve the controllability of action frame generation in the egocentric view using diffusion models and visual instruction tuning.
question.d: Current datasets and methods for human-object interaction (HOI) modeling are limited to single-person scenarios, lacking the complexity of real-world social settings involving multiple humans and objects. The HOI-M 3 dataset addresses this gap by providing a comprehensive collection of interactions, enabling advancements in data-driven motion capture and generation for complex scenarios.

title: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness
abstract: Whether current or near-term AI systems could be conscious is a topic of scientific interest and increasing public concern. This report argues for, and exemplifies, a rigorous and empirically grounded approach to AI consciousness: assessing existing AI systems in detail, in light of our best-supported neuroscientific theories of consciousness. We survey several prominent scientific theories of consciousness, including recurrent processing theory, global workspace theory, higherorder theories, predictive processing, and attention schema theory. From these theories we derive "indicator properties" of consciousness, elucidated in computational terms that allow us to assess AI systems for these properties. We use these indicator properties to assess several recent AI systems, and we discuss how future systems might implement them. Our analysis suggests that no current AI systems are conscious, but also suggests that there are no obvious technical barriers to building AI systems which satisfy these indicators. 1

question.a: The research addresses the need for a formal measure of goal-directedness in AI systems, which is crucial for understanding and mitigating risks associated with advanced AI. Current achievements include the development of agentic systems, but there's a lack of formal methods to measure their goal-directed behavior. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing a philosophically motivated measure that can be applied to known or unknown utility functions, contributing to the field by enabling better behavioral evaluations and governance of AI systems.
question.b: Traditional metrics for evaluating AI-synthesized images, such as LPIPS and CLIP-Score, are often task-agnostic and lack explainability, limiting their effectiveness. Human evaluations, while insightful, face scalability and subjectivity issues. VIESCORE addresses these limitations by providing a task-aware, explainable automated evaluation method that aligns with human judgment.
question.c: The current discourse on artificial intelligence consciousness often lacks a rigorous scientific framework, leading to ambiguous claims about AI capabilities. Many discussions fail to align with established neuroscientific theories, creating a disconnect between theoretical understanding and practical assessment. This paper addresses this gap by defining "indicator properties" derived from prominent theories of consciousness, facilitating a structured evaluation of AI systems regarding their potential conscious attributes. Such clarity is essential for advancing both research and public understanding in this emerging field.
question.d: Current AI models lack the systematic organization of units seen in the brain, where nearby neurons tend to share similar functions. Past efforts to introduce topography into AI models have often led to trade-offs between topography and task performance. This research aims to bridge the gap between biological and artificial systems by developing a method that integrates topography into AI models without compromising their performance, thereby advancing the development of models that more closely emulate the computational strategies of the human brain.

title: X3D: Expanding Architectures for Efficient Video Recognition
abstract: This paper presents X3D, a family of efficient video networks that progressively expand a tiny 2D image classification architecture along multiple network axes, in space, time, width and depth. Inspired by feature selection methods in machine learning, a simple stepwise network expansion approach is employed that expands a single axis in each step, such that good accuracy to complexity trade-off is achieved. To expand X3D to a specific target complexity, we perform progressive forward expansion followed by backward contraction. X3D achieves state-of-the-art performance while requiring 4.8× and 5.5× fewer multiply-adds and parameters for similar accuracy as previous work. Our most surprising finding is that networks with high spatiotemporal resolution can perform well, while being extremely light in terms of network width and parameters. We report competitive accuracy at unprecedented efficiency on video classification and detection benchmarks. Code will be available at:

question.a: Current neural rendering techniques for constructing FVVs require complete video sequences for offline training and cannot achieve real-time rendering, limiting their practical applications. 3DGStream addresses these limitations by enabling fast on-the-fly per-frame reconstruction and real-time rendering, significantly reducing training time and storage requirements.
question.b: The field of 3D computer vision lacks robust performance across tasks due to the scarcity of 3D data and difficulty in obtaining quality annotations. The paper addresses these challenges by proposing a novel 3D pre-training approach that utilizes existing 2D networks and large-scale multi-view datasets, aiming to bridge the gap between 2D and 3D feature extraction and enable efficient multi-modal queries.
question.c: Current video recognition architectures often struggle to balance accuracy with computational efficiency, particularly under varying constraints. Despite advancements, existing networks frequently generate excessive redundancy across spatial, temporal, and depth dimensions, impeding broader application. This paper seeks to fill this pivotal gap by introducing X3D, a novel network design that efficiently expands a foundational architecture, enhancing performance without overwhelming resource requirements, thus enabling effective video classification across diverse operational contexts.
question.d: Video transformers are slow to train due to the large number of input tokens, many of which are redundant. Existing methods to reduce input tokens either have significant overhead, require dataset-specific tuning, or decrease accuracy. RLT addresses these limitations by being content-aware, requiring no tuning for different datasets, and being fast with negligible overhead, aiming to significantly accelerate and further scale video understanding.

title: Negative Frames Matter in Egocentric Visual Query 2D Localization
abstract: The recently released Ego4D dataset and benchmark Our study is based on the three-stage baseline introduced in the Episodic Memory benchmark. The baseline solves the problem by detection and tracking: detect the similar objects in all the frames, then run a tracker from the most confident detection result. In the VQ2D challenge, we identified two limitations of the current baseline. (1) The training configuration has redundant computation. Although the training set has millions of instances, most of them are repetitive and the number of unique object is only around 14.6k. The repeated gradient computation of the same object lead to an inefficient training; (2) The false positive rate is high on background frames. This is due to the distribution gap between training and evaluation. During training, the model is only able to see the clean, stable, and labeled frames, but the egocentric videos also have noisy, blurry, or unlabeled background frames. To this end, we developed a more efficient and effective solution. Concretely, we bring the training loop from 15 days to less than 24 hours, and we achieve 0.17% spatialtemporal AP, which is 31% higher than the baseline. Our solution got the first ranking on the public leaderboard. Our code is publicly available at

question.a: The field of 3D computer vision lacks robust performance across tasks due to the scarcity of 3D data and difficulty in obtaining quality annotations. The paper addresses these challenges by proposing a novel 3D pre-training approach that utilizes existing 2D networks and large-scale multi-view datasets, aiming to bridge the gap between 2D and 3D feature extraction and enable efficient multi-modal queries.
question.b: Current Large Language Models (LLMs) and Visual Large Language Models (VLLMs) have limitations in providing directly applicable instructions for human skill transfer and in generating images that align with the user's egocentric perspective. The paper addresses these limitations by proposing a method to enrich action descriptions and improve the controllability of action frame generation in the egocentric view using diffusion models and visual instruction tuning.
question.c: The current baseline for egocentric visual query 2D localization, while effective, suffers from significant inefficiencies due to redundant computation and high false positive rates associated with background frames. These limitations exist because the training configuration fails to account for the repetitive nature of data and the distribution discrepancy between training and evaluation. This research directly addresses these challenges, aiming to enhance training efficiency and improve model performance in real-world contexts.
question.d: Current egocentric pose estimation methods struggle with accuracy due to self-occlusion and limited camera views. While joint heatmaps improve 2D pose estimation, converting these to 3D poses remains inaccurate. This paper aims to enhance the accuracy of 3D pose estimation in egocentric setups by introducing a new method that effectively utilizes joint heatmaps and skeletal information.

title: On the Relationship Between Explanation and Prediction: A Causal View
abstract: Being able to provide explanations for a model's decision has become a central requirement for the development, deployment, and adoption of machine learning models. However, we are yet to understand what explanation methods can and cannot do. How do upstream factors such as data, model prediction, hyperparameters, and random initialization influence downstream explanations? While previous work raised concerns that explanations (E) may have little relationship with the prediction (Y ), there is a lack of conclusive study to quantify this relationship. Our work borrows tools from causal inference to systematically assay this relationship. More specifically, we study the relationship between E and Y by measuring the treatment effect when intervening on their causal ancestors, i.e., on hyperparameters and inputs used to generate saliency-based Es or Y s. Our results suggest that the relationships between E and Y is far from ideal. In fact, the gap between 'ideal' case only increase in higher-performing modelsmodels that are likely to be deployed. Our work is a promising first step towards providing a quantitative measure of the relationship between E and Y , which could also inform the future development of methods for E with a quantitative metric.

question.a: The relationship between model explanations and predictions remains inadequately understood, despite its critical importance in machine learning adoption. Existing studies highlight that explanations may not correlate well with predictions, yet there has been insufficient quantitative analysis of this relationship. By exploring how upstream factors, such as hyperparameters and input data, impact downstream explanations, this paper aims to provide foundational insights and encourage future methodological development in explanation practices within machine learning.
question.b: Current methods for explaining NLP model predictions often rely on input features like words, which can be less informative due to their discrete and context-lacking nature. LACOAT addresses this by using latent concepts from the training data to provide more contextually enriched explanations of model predictions, improving interpretability and trustworthiness of AI systems.
question.c: AI models are increasingly used in safety-critical domains like healthcare, but their adoption is hindered by limited transparency and robustness. Current explainability methods are rarely evaluated with real-world users, leading to uncertainty about their practical utility. This paper addresses the gap by conducting a user study with 85 healthcare practitioners to assess how different explanations impact human-AI collaboration in a clinical setting, especially when AI predictions and explanations are imperfect.
question.d: The increasing use of neural networks, particularly large language models, has heightened the demand for interpretability to ensure reliable and ethical deployment. Existing explanation methods often suffer from high computational cost, difficult-to-interpret explanations, and potentially unfaithful representations of the model's decision-making process. This paper addresses these limitations by developing a single model that generates faithful and interpretable explanations alongside its predictions, thereby avoiding the instability and inefficiencies of traditional multi-player rationalized models.

title: Revisiting Fundamentals of Experience Replay
abstract: Experience replay is central to off-policy algorithms in deep reinforcement learning (RL), but there remain significant gaps in our understanding. We therefore present a systematic and extensive analysis of experience replay in Q-learning methods, focusing on two fundamental properties: the replay capacity and the ratio of learning updates to experience collected (replay ratio). Our additive and ablative studies upend conventional wisdom around experience replay -greater capacity is found to substantially increase the performance of certain algorithms, while leaving others unaffected. Counterintuitively we show that theoretically ungrounded, uncorrected n-step returns are uniquely beneficial while other techniques confer limited benefit for sifting through larger memory. Separately, by directly controlling the replay ratio we contextualize previous observations in the literature and empirically measure its importance across a variety of deep RL algorithms. Finally, we conclude by testing a set of hypotheses on the nature of these performance benefits.

question.a: Deep reinforcement learning has achieved significant success but struggles with generalization to unseen environments. Current UED methods either rely on learning-based approaches, which are unstable and lack diversity, or replay-based methods, which are sample inefficient. The proposed ADD method addresses these limitations by combining the strengths of both approaches, using diffusion models to generate diverse and challenging environments efficiently.
question.b: Current online reinforcement learning methods use replay buffers to store and reuse experience, but uniform replay is inefficient as not all transitions are equally relevant for learning. Prioritization can lead to overfitting due to the rarity of useful samples. PGR addresses these issues by using generative models to densify past experience and guide generation towards more useful parts of an agent's history, improving learning efficiency and reducing overfitting.
question.c: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) faces challenges such as distributional shift and overestimation errors due to the lack of interaction with the environment. Existing methods like Conservative Q-learning (CQL) reduce overestimation but introduce unnecessary estimation bias, leading to performance degradation. EPQ aims to address these limitations by selectively penalizing states that cause estimation errors, thereby improving the accuracy of policy evaluation in offline RL.
question.d: While experience replay is integral to off-policy deep reinforcement learning algorithms, significant gaps remain in its fundamental understanding, particularly regarding replay capacity and learning update ratios. Current literature often lacks a systematic assessment of these properties, which may lead to misconceptions about their impact on algorithm performance. This paper aims to clarify these issues, offering insights that may reconcile conflicting findings and advance practical applications of experience replay in deep reinforcement learning.

title: Don't Blame the ELBO! A Linear VAE Perspective on Posterior Collapse
abstract: Posterior collapse in Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) arises when the variational posterior distribution closely matches the prior for a subset of latent variables. This paper presents a simple and intuitive explanation for posterior collapse through the analysis of linear VAEs and their direct correspondence with Probabilistic PCA (pPCA). We explain how posterior collapse may occur in pPCA due to local maxima in the log marginal likelihood. Unexpectedly, we prove that the ELBO objective for the linear VAE does not introduce additional spurious local maxima relative to log marginal likelihood. We show further that training a linear VAE with exact variational inference recovers an identifiable global maximum corresponding to the principal component directions. Empirically, we find that our linear analysis is predictive even for high-capacity, non-linear VAEs and helps explain the relationship between the observation noise, local maxima, and posterior collapse in deep Gaussian VAEs. * Intern at Google Brain Code available at

question.a: Understanding the loss landscape of neural networks is crucial for explaining why local gradient methods find nearly optimal parameters. While previous works have shown the loss landscape to be 'benign' in certain aspects, there's a need for a deeper mathematical understanding of the global optimum's structure, especially in the context of regularized networks. This paper addresses this gap by analyzing the loss landscape through convex reformulations and duality, providing insights into the phase transitions in connectivity and the uniqueness of solutions.
question.b: Current latent variable models in neuroscience, such as VAEs, focus on inferring low-dimensional representations but often fail to generate realistic and diverse samples of neural activity, especially when conditioning on external covariates. LDNS addresses this gap by leveraging the strengths of diffusion models for high-fidelity generation and autoencoders for latent space inference, enabling the generation of realistic neural spiking data conditioned on behavioral or task-related information.
question.c: Posterior collapse presents a significant challenge in the training of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), as highlighted by the tendency for variational posteriors to converge too closely to their priors. Despite extensive investigation, the underlying reasons for this phenomenon remain inadequately understood, particularly in complex models. This paper aims to clarify the connection between the ELBO objective and local maxima in the marginal likelihood for linear VAEs, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of posterior collapse and its implications for model performance.
question.d: Neural collapse (NC) is a phenomenon observed in DNNs where the feature vectors of the training data in the penultimate layer collapse to a single vector per class, forming a highly symmetric structure. While previous research has focused on the unconstrained features model (UFM), which is data-agnostic, this paper addresses the limitations of UFM by studying DNNs with end-to-end training. The paper aims to contribute to the field by proving the first end-to-end guarantees for neural collapse in deep networks trained via gradient descent with weight decay.

title: projUNN: efficient method for training deep networks with unitary matrices
abstract: In learning with recurrent or very deep feed-forward networks, employing unitary matrices in each layer can be very effective at maintaining long-range stability. However, restricting network parameters to be unitary typically comes at the cost of expensive parameterizations or increased training runtime. We propose instead an efficient method based on rank-k updates -or their rank-k approximation -that maintains performance at a nearly optimal training runtime. We introduce two variants of this method, named Direct (projUNN-D) and Tangent (projUNN-T) projected Unitary Neural Networks, that can parameterize full N -dimensional unitary or orthogonal matrices with a training runtime scaling as O(kN 2 ). Our method either projects low-rank gradients onto the closest unitary matrix (projUNN-T) or transports unitary matrices in the direction of the low-rank gradient (projUNN-D). Even in the fastest setting (k = 1), projUNN is able to train a model's unitary parameters to reach comparable performances against baseline implementations. In recurrent neural network settings, projUNN closely matches or exceeds benchmarked results from prior unitary neural networks. Finally, we preliminarily explore projUNN in training orthogonal convolutional neural networks, which are currently unable to outperform state of the art models but can potentially enhance stability and robustness at large depth.
